messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fifteen months ago, Duy was working on a rooftop cooling tower at a downtown logistics warehouse when a high-pressure refrigerant line cracked without warning. A dense, sweet-smelling vapor rolled across the grating, stinging his eyes and burning his throat before he could pull his disposable mask tighter. A hazmat crew pulled him clear, and though his lungs healed, his nervous system never reset. A visceral certainty took hold: invisible threats could fill a room without warning, and nothing was truly sealed against them. Over the following months, Duy’s body never stopped bracing for the next exposure. His shoulders remained permanently knotted, his jaw clenched, and his breath stayed shallow, as if his physiology was still trying to filter a toxic atmosphere that wasn’t there. When he returned to his own home, he found himself pacing the perimeter at night, turning each deadbolt three times and lifting every window sash to verify it was sealed. When his wife would rest her hand on his shoulder and tell him the air inside was perfectly clean, Duy would nod politely but feel nothing but a cold, impenetrable certainty in his chest. He had come to believe that reassurance was just another layer of paint over a leak, and that silence from others did not mean safety—it only meant the threat had not yet announced itself. Because his body stayed locked in that perpetual state of alarm, Duy slowly began to construct a life that kept the pressure valves from ever rising again. The constant physiological readiness made stillness unbearable; the moment he allowed himself to relax on the couch, a terrifying certainty took hold that his guard was down and an unseen vapor would slip through a seal he no longer trusted. He began avoiding rooms where he could not see an exit, and he started turning down work assignments that required navigating tight mechanical rooms. He avoided stressors of any kind, recalibrating his schedule to eliminate urgency, skipping overtime, and quietly requesting lateral transfers. As the weeks turned to months, the certainty that the air was untrustworthy only deepened, and the avoidance behaviors only grew stricter. Every time he skipped a stressful shift or checked a lock one more time, the temporary relief confirmed his worst fear: he had to keep his guard up forever, and the loop of suspicion and restriction only widened. At work, this recalibration became impossible to hide. As an HVAC technician who spent his days crawling through ceiling plenums and kneeling beside roaring compressors, Duy found himself unable to enter the narrow access tunnels where the air grew stale and heavy. He began claiming he could not fit in the ductwork and refused to work near chemical storage rooms. His foreman grew frustrated as Duy’s reliability eroded, noting how he would sit in the open garage for hours instead of going upstairs to watch television with his wife. His spouse soon realized he was no longer sleeping in the guest room without a space heater and a cracked window, and she began interpreting his flinches at the central air handler’s mechanical rumble as proof that he was slowly strangling their life together. By the time he finally walked into the clinic, Duy’s PCL-5 score of seventy-three was no longer just a number—it was the sum of sixteen months spent bracing for an invisible cloud that never left. What brought him through the door was not a single crisis, but the quiet exhaustion of watching his own world shrink. He had stopped driving past industrial parks, he could barely sit through dinner with friends when they mentioned their new home renovation, and he no longer trusted his own breathing. He sat in the therapist’s chair now, hands resting flat on his knees to keep them from reaching for the door handle, hoping the session might finally offer him a way to believe the air around him was just air again.
